'''''Hibiscus mutabilis''''', also known as the '''cotton rose''' or '''rosemallow'''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hibiscus mutabilis L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:560549-1 |access-date=2026-02-21 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>''',''' a plant long cultivated for its showy flowers. Originally native to southern [[China]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibiscus mutabilis L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science|url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:560549-1|access-date=2021-02-26|website=Plants of the World Online|language=en}}</ref> where it is known as 木芙蓉, ("Mùfúróng")[http://www.fpcn.net/a/guanmu/20131016/Hibiscus_mutabilis.html] it is now found on all continents except [[Antarctica]]. It is a mallow (family [[Malvaceae]]) not a true rose (family [[Rosaceae]]). Alternative names in parts of the United States are '''Confederate rose''' and '''Dixie rosemallow'''.

==Description==
Cotton roses are [[semi-deciduous]] with palmately lobed leaves. They tend to be large shrubs or treelike in [[Hardiness zone|zones 9 and 10]], though they have a more modest shrub-like appearance more north. Stems and [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s feature dense stellate and glandular hairs.<ref>[https://sown.com.au/hibiscus-mutabilis-malvaceae-cotton-rose-confederate-rose-cotton-rosemallow/#:~:text=Semi%2Ddeciduous%20shrub%20or%20small,dark%20pink%20in%20the%20evening. Hibiscus mutabilis (MALVACEAE) Cotton Rose, Confederate Rose, Cotton Rosemallow] by Sown. Retrieved 8 June 2024.</ref> 

Flowers can be double or single and are {{convert|4-6|in|cm|abbr=on}} in diameter; they open white or pink, and change to deep red by evening. The 'Rubra' variety has red flowers. Single blooming flowers are generally cup-shaped. Bloom season usually lasts from summer through fall. When it does not freeze, the cotton rose can reach heights of {{convert|12-15|ft|abbr=on}} with a woody trunk. However, a much bushier plant {{convert|5-6|ft|abbr=on}} high is more typical and provides more flowering. 

The flowers are attractive to [[Pollinator|pollinators]], including the specialized [[bee]] ''[[Ptilothrix bombiformis]].''<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hibiscus mutabilis (Confederate Rose, Cotton Rose) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/hibiscus-mutabilis/|access-date=2021-02-26|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Propagation by root cuttings is the easiest and is done in early spring, but cuttings can be taken at almost any time. These plants have a very fast growth rate. The cotton rose can thrive in the southern parts of the United States, leading to its association with the 1861 to 1865 secessionist movement known as the American [[Confederate States of America|confederacy]], hence the alternative name in some areas. It grows nicely in full sun or partial shade, and prefers rich, well-drained soil.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/southerngarden/hibiscus.html |title=William C. Welch: "Hardy Hibiscus", Texas A&M University |access-date=2006-12-24 |archive-date=2010-12-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101202010314/http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/southerngarden/hibiscus.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In cultivation in the [[United Kingdom|UK]], ''Hibiscus mutabilis'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/40524/Hibiscus-mutabilis/Details | title = ''Hibiscus mutabilis'' | website = www.rhs.org | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 23 August 2020}}</ref>

==Floral color change==
[[File:Hibiscus mutabilis, changing colors.jpg|thumb|Changing colors of the flower during a day]]
[[File:Li_Di_-_Red_and_White_Cotton_Roses_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg|thumb|''Red and White Cotton Roses'', a historical painting by [[Li Di]] (李迪), which shows the flowers with changing colors. China, [[Song dynasty]], 1197 AD]]
[[Floral color change]] occurs in ''H. mutabilis'' when flowers are white in the morning, turning pink during noon and red in the evening of the same day. Under laboratory conditions, the color change of the [[Petal|petals]] was slower than that of flowers under outdoor conditions.<ref name=Wong>{{cite journal | author = Wong, S.K. | author2 = Lim, Y.Y. | author3 = Chan, E.W.C. | date = 2009 | title = Antioxidant properties of ''Hibiscus'': species variation, altitudinal change, coastal influence and floral colour change | journal = Journal of Tropical Forest Science | volume = 21 | issue = 4 | pages = 307–315 | url = http://info.frim.gov.my/cfdocs/infocenter_application/jtfsonline/jtfs/V21n4/307-315.pdf | access-date = 2010-02-09 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110722232838/http://info.frim.gov.my/cfdocs/infocenter_application/jtfsonline/jtfs/V21n4/307-315.pdf | archive-date = 2011-07-22 | url-status = dead }}</ref> Temperature may be an important factor, affecting the rate of color change as white flowers kept in the refrigerator remain white until they are taken out to warm up, whereupon they slowly turn pink.<ref>{{cite book | author = Ng, F.S.P. | date = 2006 | title = Tropical Horticulture and Gardening | publisher = Clearwater Publications | location = Kuala Lumpur | isbn = 983-42954-0-5}}</ref>

The red flowers remain on plants for several days before they abort.<ref name=Wong/> Weight of a single detached flower was {{convert|15.6|g|abbr=on}} when white, {{convert|12.7|g|abbr=on}} when pink and {{convert|11.0|g|abbr=on}} when red. [[Anthocyanin]] content of red flowers was three times that of pink flowers and eight times that of white flowers. There was a significant increase in [[Phenolic acid|phenolic]] content with color change. Overall ranking of [[antioxidant]] properties of ''H. mutabilis'' flowers was red > pink > white.

Subramanian and Nair postulated that anthocyanins in pink and red flowers of ''H. mutabilis'' are synthesized independently since there is no reduction in phenolic content.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Subramanian, S.S. | author2 = Nair, A.G.R. | date = 1970 | title = A note on the colour change of the flowers of ''Hibiscus mutabilis'' | journal = Current Science | volume = 39 | issue = 14 | pages = 323–324}}</ref> However, Lowry suggested that anthocyanins are formed through direct conversion from [[flavonols]] as they have structural similarities.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Lowry, J.B. | date = 1976 | title = Floral anthocyanins of some Malesian ''Hibiscus'' species | journal = Phytochemistry | volume = 15 | issue = 9 | pages = 1395–1396 | doi=10.1016/s0031-9422(00)97124-3}}</ref>
